weights.description: Per-signal weights in the risk score. `deep`: adding a signal's weight in a repo file does not drop the signals you weighted at home.

^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$.description: Per-signal weights in the risk score. `deep`: adding a signal's weight in a repo file does not drop the signals you weighted at home.

rss.description: The RSS budgets. Per ADR-004 §11.8 these are *never* scaled by a machine factor, so the only knob is the size class.

analyzer_working_set.description: Per-analyzer working set; an analyzer needing more must stream or say it is running in the background lane.

mib.description: Per-analyzer working set; an analyzer needing more must stream or say it is running in the background lane.

cold_index_peak_mib.description: Cold-index peak RSS budget, graph lane included.

daemon.description: Daemon at idle plus one in-flight warm index.

mib.description: Daemon at idle plus one in-flight warm index.

sqlite_page_cache.description: `PRAGMA cache_size` per connection: fixed per connection, not per table.

mib.description: `PRAGMA cache_size` per connection: fixed per connection, not per table.

tui.description: Steady-state TUI with a warm store. Never scaled by a machine factor (ADR-004 §11.8): memory budgets are not time budgets.

mib.description: Steady-state TUI with a warm store. Never scaled by a machine factor (ADR-004 §11.8): memory budgets are not time budgets.

scorecard.description: What the architecture score is made of: the five weights, the window a per-window score covers, how much movement still counts as flat, how many revisions a printed trend keeps, and the four published constants the curves divide by. The curve *shapes* are not knobs — they are the model — so every number a reviewer can recompute by hand stays recomputable after a tune. `fathom architecture --explain` prints what is in force. `e3.9`.

alert_below.description: The score below which the report says `alert: true`. This is a *reported flag*, not an exit code: the CI gate is `fathom check` (reco-ngk), and two places deciding 'under 50 is a failure' is how a gate and a dashboard end up disagreeing about the same run. `e3.9`.

api_knee.description: How many vanished exports score API hygiene at a half. The API term has no honest denominator at the graph's grain, so it uses a knee — `n / (n + k)` — and this is the published `k`. `e3.9`.

coupling_ceiling.description: The mean dependency edges per module that scores as fully coupled: the denominator of the coupling share is modules x this ceiling. Published so a reader can redo the division; the basis line prints both numbers. `e3.9`.

flat_within.description: How many points of movement still counts as *no movement*. The arithmetic is exact, but a score is a ratio over a graph that moves one module at a time, and 'the architecture moved 1 point this week' would be an invitation to read noise as news. The band is printed beside every verdict, never applied silently. `e3.9`.

hotspot_bar.description: The hotspot score at or above which a module counts as pressure in the fifth dimension. It is the same 0–100 scale `fathom hotspots` prints, so the scorecard and the table agree about what a hot module is. `e3.9`.

trend_cap.description: How many plotted points a trend series may hold. Older revisions are thinned, the oldest and newest ends are always kept, and the report prints how many rows were read and dropped — so memory is bounded by this number rather than by the repository's history. `e3.9`.

weight.description: How much of the score is owed to respecting the layering rules this repository wrote down. The largest default, because it is the one dimension with a *written rule* behind it: a violation is a finding a reviewer can act on. With no rules declared the dimension refuses rather than flattering, and its weight leaves the denominator. `e3.9`.

acyclicity.description: How much of the score is owed to how much of the graph sits inside a loop nobody budgeted. Debt with an owner and an expiry is not counted: the ratchet already forgave it, and counting it again would call the day you wrote the baseline a day the architecture degraded. `e3.9`.

api.description: How much of the score is owed to what this episode did to the contracts other code compiles against. Smallest when the store can only see the module graph's export grain — a signature change that kept its name is invisible there — and a coarse signal should not be handed a fine share of the verdict. `e3.9`.

boundaries.description: How much of the score is owed to respecting the layering rules this repository wrote down. The largest default, because it is the one dimension with a *written rule* behind it: a violation is a finding a reviewer can act on. With no rules declared the dimension refuses rather than flattering, and its weight leaves the denominator. `e3.9`.

coupling.description: How much of the score is owed to how far an average module reaches. Coupling describes a shape, not a mistake — a well-designed graph can be a coupled one — so it is weighted under the two rule-backed dimensions on purpose. `e3.9`.

hotspots.description: How much of the score is owed to how many modules are expensive to change and widely felt. A hot module is usually the load-bearing wall, so this term says where attention is owed rather than that someone was wrong. `e3.9`.

window.description: How many revisions a per-window score covers, and the churn window the hotspot term reads. Thirty is the window every other 'recent' measure in Fathom already uses, so the scorecard and the heat map are talking about the same month. `e3.9`.

store.description: WAL ceiling and the soft store-size ceiling `doctor` warns at.

size.description: Soft store-size ceiling: `fathom doctor` warns at this size. A warning, never a refusal — refusing to write would lose the review ledger's context.

mib.description: Soft store-size ceiling: `fathom doctor` warns at this size. A warning, never a refusal — refusing to write would lose the review ledger's context.

wal_cap.description: WAL size at which the writer warns and forces a passive checkpoint.

mib.description: WAL size at which the writer warns and forces a passive checkpoint.

structure.description: Where an episode's code landed. The thresholds that decide when a set of pairings is a moved directory, a split or a flattening, the weights behind the structure-churn score, and one switch per finding kind. `fathom structure definition` prints these numbers as sentences.

card.description: Directory rows a card prints before it says how many more there are and which verb lists them. A cap that names its remainder, never a truncation without a trace.

max_dirs.description: Directory rows a card prints before it says how many more there are and which verb lists them. A cap that names its remainder, never a truncation without a trace.

max_evidence.description: Evidence lines printed per finding, with the remainder counted and named rather than dropped. Every line is always in `--json` and in `fathom structure findings`.

max_stories.description: Structural stories a card prints before counting the rest. Six is more stories than an honest episode produces; a seventh usually means one directory was renamed in six places, which is one story, told six times.

churn.description: Churn weight: share of the episode's files that changed directory. The five weights are normalised, so what matters is their ratio; this and `moved_lines` together make half the score, because `most of this episode was a move` is the claim the score exists to make.

band.description: Below this churn score the episode is `local`: it changed contents where they already were. Set from the 20-file local-change fixture, which scores 0.000; the band exists so the card can say `local` instead of making the reviewer read five components.

local.description: Below this churn score the episode is `local`: it changed contents where they already were. Set from the 20-file local-change fixture, which scores 0.000; the band exists so the card can say `local` instead of making the reviewer read five components.

structural.description: At or above this the episode is `structural`: the tree itself moved. The 20-file cross-tree reshuffle fixture scores 0.900 and the 20-file local-change fixture 0.000, so the bar sits far from both rather than between two close calls. Between the two bands is `transitional`, and the card says that rather than rounding to a verdict.

depth_scale.description: Mean-depth change at which the shape component saturates. Four levels is where `the tree got deeper` has stopped being an incidental effect of where this episode's files landed and has become the change itself.

story_ceiling.description: Stories at which the story component saturates. A third story is not 50% worse than a second - it is the same story about a third folder - so a linear term would let a wide rename out-score a deep one.

weight.description: Churn weight: share of the episode's files that changed directory. The five weights are normalised, so what matters is their ratio; this and `moved_lines` together make half the score, because `most of this episode was a move` is the claim the score exists to make.

directory_churn.description: Churn weight: directories added and removed over directories the episode touched. Weighed below the mobility terms because a rename creates and deletes folders as a side effect of what already counted as a move.

moved_files.description: Churn weight: share of the episode's files that changed directory. The five weights are normalised, so what matters is their ratio; this and `moved_lines` together make half the score, because `most of this episode was a move` is the claim the score exists to make.

moved_lines.description: Churn weight: share of the episode's lines that travelled with a move. File counts alone let a one-line edit to a thousand files look like a reorganisation; line counts alone let one 5 000-line generated file moving look like one. Both are in, at equal weight.

shape_shift.description: Churn weight: how far the tree's own shape metrics (mean and maximum depth, top-N concentration) moved. The smallest weight, because depth can change a lot in an episode that moved nothing; this is the tie-breaker, not the headline.

stories.description: Churn weight: the structural stories found, saturating at `structure.churn.story_ceiling`. A story is a counted claim with evidence attached, not a feeling, so it is worth a fifth of the score on its own.

code_classes.description: Which taxonomy classes (`e0.9`, `e2.1`) count as code when the card measures where the code lives. `docs`, `config` and `generated` are out: a folder of markdown moving house is real, but it is not the same concentration claim as 4 000 lines of source changing home.

concentration.description: Growth in the top-N code share that is worth a `concentration-up` row. Smaller moves are what ordinary growth does to a tree; fifteen points is the tree getting one big folder.

delta.description: Growth in the top-N code share that is worth a `concentration-up` row. Smaller moves are what ordinary growth does to a tree; fifteen points is the tree getting one big folder.

depth.description: Mean directory-depth growth that is worth a `nesting-deepened` row. Half a level over one episode is where a tree has stopped being shallow by accident.

max_delta.description: Maximum-depth growth that earns the same row on its own, because one branch pushed two levels deeper is a review problem even when the mean barely moved.

mean_delta.description: Mean directory-depth growth that is worth a `nesting-deepened` row. Half a level over one episode is where a tree has stopped being shallow by accident.

findings.description: A whole directory - its files and its inner folders - now lives under a different parent. Nothing inside it changed, so the reviewable content of the episode is the move itself. `e2.3`.

churn_high.description: The structure-churn score reached `structure.churn.band.structural`: the agent reorganised the tree. The card prints the score with all five components beside it, so this row is a number and not a vibe. `e2.3`.

concentration_up.description: The share of code living in the top-N directories grew by the configured delta: the tree is getting one big folder. `e2.3`.

directory_added.description: A new directory now holds files. Loud enough to notice, quiet enough not to compete with the move that explains it. `e2.3`.

directory_flattened.description: A directory moved its files up into an ancestor and vanished, so the tree is one level shallower where it used to be. `e2.3`.

directory_removed.description: A directory that held files holds none. Reported even when its files were moved rather than deleted, because a removed directory is also a removed namespace and a stale import path. `e2.3`.

files_moved.description: Files changed directory without forming one of the four named shapes - a partial move, a move with a rename on the way, or a move out of a directory that still has files in it. `e2.3`.

module_split.description: One directory's files now live in two or more destinations. A split is where responsibility moved, which is the reviewable question, and the destinations are named. `e2.3`.

move_unconfirmed.description: Some pairing behind this answer was inferred from bytes, or handed over below `structure.move.fact_bar`, rather than asserted by git - so the directory rows built on it inherit that uncertainty and are listed instead of silently believed. `e2.3`.

nesting_deepened.description: Average (or maximum) directory depth grew by the configured delta. Deep trees are how a review starts hiding things from itself. `e2.3`.

package_renamed.description: A directory changed name in place with its contents intact, so every import of it moved and none of its logic did. `e2.3`.

subtree_moved.description: A whole directory - its files and its inner folders - now lives under a different parent. Nothing inside it changed, so the reviewable content of the episode is the move itself. `e2.3`.

flatten.description: How many directory levels a move has to climb for the shape to be flattening rather than an ordinary move sideways. One is `went up at least one level, and the folder behind it is gone`, which is the shape.

min_levels.description: How many directory levels a move has to climb for the shape to be flattening rather than an ordinary move sideways. One is `went up at least one level, and the folder behind it is gone`, which is the shape.

metrics.description: The N in `share of code in the top-N directories`. Three because that is the width the review question is asked with: top-1 measures one folder, top-10 measures the whole tree and separates nothing.

top_dirs.description: The N in `share of code in the top-N directories`. Three because that is the width the review question is asked with: top-1 measures one folder, top-10 measures the whole tree and separates nothing.

move.description: Pairings a whole-directory story (`package-renamed`, `subtree-move`, `module- split`, `directory-flattened`) has to be built from. Below this, two files changing folder is a `files-moved` row, not a reorganisation of the tree - and a card that called every two-file move a reorganisation would be noisier than the file list it replaced.

fact_bar.description: Confidence at or above which a caller-supplied pairing counts as a fact rather than a guess. Deliberately the same number as `rename.fact_bar`, which spike s4 measured on real histories: at git's shipped 0.50 the pairing engine asserts a named decoy, at 0.75 it ships nothing false. A structure card that trusted pairings git would not is a card that lies about where code landed.

infer_content.description: When the caller supplies no pairings, infer them from bytes (same basename, similarity at or above `structure.move.min_similarity`). Turning this off makes the answer strictly narrower - no inferred moves, and the card says so - which is the right setting for a reviewer who will only act on what git asserted.

min_files.description: Pairings a whole-directory story (`package-renamed`, `subtree-move`, `module- split`, `directory-flattened`) has to be built from. Below this, two files changing folder is a `files-moved` row, not a reorganisation of the tree - and a card that called every two-file move a reorganisation would be noisier than the file list it replaced.

min_share.description: Share of a directory's files that must have moved for the directory itself to be called moved. 1.0 demands a perfect sweep and loses every move with one straggler file; 0.0 calls any relocation a whole-directory move. 0.6 is `most of it`, which is what a reviewer means by `they moved the package`.

min_similarity.description: Line similarity required to accept an inferred pairing, computed exactly rather than sketched. Used only to accept or refuse a pairing, never printed as a similarity verdict of its own. Half the lines shared is where `the same file, edited` stops being a guess.

require_emptied.description: Additionally require that the source directory holds no files afterwards. On, a move is a move. Off, a directory that shipped most of its files and kept three still reads as moved, which is true of the files and misleading about the directory.

split.description: Destinations a module split needs. One destination is a move, and calling a move a split tells the reviewer responsibility was divided when nothing of the sort happened.

min_destinations.description: Destinations a module split needs. One destination is a move, and calling a move a split tells the reviewer responsibility was divided when nothing of the sort happened.

min_files_per_destination.description: Files a destination needs to count as one arm of a split. One is the natural floor and the wrong one: a directory of 17 files with a single stray in a new folder is a move of 16 plus a `files-moved` row, not a two-arm split of the module.

taxonomy.description: Assert what a set of paths IS, relative to the built-in table: one open map keyed by class. The engine and the built-ins are `reco-5vz`'s; only the overrides live here.

classes.description: One entry per taxonomy class: globs that assert paths ARE that class, outranking the built-in table because a user layer beats the defaults layer. `generated = ["src/gen/**"]` demotes hand-written-looking code; `source = ["vendor/our-fork/**"]` promotes vendored-looking code. `recommender/taxonomy/builtins.py` owns the built-ins; this key only overrides them, which is what `fathom explain <path>` prints as the winning layer.

^(?:source|test|docs|config|schema|migra.description: One entry per taxonomy class: globs that assert paths ARE that class, outranking the built-in table because a user layer beats the defaults layer. `generated = ["src/gen/**"]` demotes hand-written-looking code; `source = ["vendor/our-fork/**"]` promotes vendored-looking code. `recommender/taxonomy/builtins.py` owns the built-ins; this key only overrides them, which is what `fathom explain <path>` prints as the winning layer.
x-fathom-open: a path-taxonomy class (`reco-5vz`); `other` is refused because asserting it is indistinguishable from matching nothing

test.description: What counts as a test, which test-surface findings fire, and the numbers that define 'new public logic, no new test'. The finding policy is here rather than in `[detectors]` because these findings are one definition with knobs, not a detector registry.

card.description: How many finding rows the card prints before it says how many more there are and which verb lists them. A cap that names the remainder, never a truncation without a trace.

max_findings.description: How many finding rows the card prints before it says how many more there are and which verb lists them. A cap that names the remainder, never a truncation without a trace.

findings.description: Report a named test case that existed in the old revision and is gone. A deletion is a first-class finding with the case name and its line, including the cases lost because the whole file went.

assertion_removed.description: Report a test case that survived but lost exact assertions and gained none.

assertion_weakened.description: Report an exact assertion replaced by a presence check on the same subject (`assert_eq!(x, 42)` → `assert!(x.is_ok())`, `expect(x).toBe(3)` → `.toBeDefined()`). The comparison is subject-to-subject, so it is about the same value both times.

focused_test.description: Report a committed `it.only`/`fit`/`fdescribe`: every other test in that file is silently not running.

test_file_removed.description: Also report the file-level row when a test file is deleted, beside the case-level rows for the tests inside it.

test_removed.description: Report a named test case that existed in the old revision and is gone. A deletion is a first-class finding with the case name and its line, including the cases lost because the whole file went.

test_skipped.description: Report a case that used to run and is now `#[ignore]`, `@pytest.mark.skip`, `xfail`, `t.Skip`, `it.skip` or `@Disabled`. A skipped test still exists and proves nothing, so it shares the channel a deletion gets.

untested_public.description: Report new public logic that no test surface in the episode covers. What 'public', 'logic' and 'covers' mean is the `test.untested.*` block below, not a hunch.

proxy.description: Stated confidence when every test surface in the episode was parsed into named cases. Printed on the card, never left implicit.

confidence.description: Stated confidence when every test surface in the episode was parsed into named cases. Printed on the card, never left implicit.

lines_only.description: Stated confidence when no test framework was found and the only honest number is a line count. Deliberately low: a line count correlates with test effort and does not measure it.

parsed.description: Stated confidence when every test surface in the episode was parsed into named cases. Printed on the card, never left implicit.

partial.description: Stated confidence when some test surface had no parser or a parser refused it: the case names are partly known, so the counts are a lower bound.

untested.description: How many non-blank body lines a new public symbol needs before the episode is said to have added logic. Below it a one-line re-export helper raises the finding; above it a small real function does not.

exclude.description: Paths the untested-public finding never fires for: example code, benches, generated helpers. `extend`, so a repository adds to the list.

mention_in_test.description: If a new symbol's name appears in lines the episode added to a test file, treat it as covered. The loosest of the three coverage tests, and the only one that catches a new function asserted inside a pre-existing test.

min_body_lines.description: How many non-blank body lines a new public symbol needs before the episode is said to have added logic. Below it a one-line re-export helper raises the finding; above it a small real function does not.

name_overlap.description: Name tokens a new test case must share with a new symbol to count as covering it (`load_snapshot` ↔ `TestSnapshotLoading` share `snapshot`).

path_overlap.description: Path-name tokens a changed test file must share with the source file (`src/store/load.rs` ↔ `tests/store_load_test.rs` share `store`, `load`). For repositories whose test layout is not worth encoding in `test.globs`.

require_logic.description: Only count a symbol as logic if its body calls, assigns, branches or returns. Off means a new `pub struct` or constant can raise the finding, which is what a repository that reviews schemas as API surface may want.

scope.description: `episode`: a covering test must be in this episode — the only thing measurable from a diff. `repo`: a symbol the repository's existing tests already mention is not flagged; needs the index to supply those mentions, and the card says so when it could not.

visibility.description: Which Rust visibilities count as public: `public` is plain `pub` only, `crate` also counts `pub(crate)`. Other languages have no equivalent, and the default refuses to guess that a crate-internal item owed the reviewer a test.

watch.description: What share of one core `fathom watch` may spend while work is flowing. Past it the poll stretches toward its ceiling and says so, because a watcher that overruns the machine it is watching is the failure this ticket exists to avoid.

cpu_share_pct.description: What share of one core `fathom watch` may spend while work is flowing. Past it the poll stretches itself toward its ceiling and says so in a notice, because a budget nobody can see is a budget nobody fails (ADR-004 §11). The idle watcher is nowhere near this: `watch.idle_cpu.pct` is the quiet-repository number.

write.description: Batching knobs for the single writer.

batch_ms.description: Also commit at this many ms, whichever comes first, so a big ingest still shows progress.

batch_rows.description: Rows per writer transaction (ADR-004 §7.3). Measured 12x versus one row per transaction, so this is not cosmetic.

mandatory_checkpoint_per_commit.description: Mandatory `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` calls per commit. Zero: measured at 0.8 % of a warm budget *per commit*.

queue_batches.description: How many normalized batches may sit between the ingest pipeline and the writer before the pipeline **waits** instead of allocating (`reco-93w`). This is the back-pressure knob: peak spine memory is roughly `write.queue_batches × commits_per_batch`, and a sink that falls behind shrinks the pipeline rather than growing it. One serializes the two stages, which costs a warm index its overlap; anything past a handful is a cache with none of a cache's accounting, so the schema caps it at 64.
